title: Model Context Protocol
lede: One protocol between every app and every tool. Watch a single request cross the channel and come back with live data.

audience.who: developers wiring an AI app to real tools for the first time
audience.leaves_knowing: build the server once and every MCP host can use it; M + N beats M × N

critique_of_obvious: The usual picture is a logo cloud with arrows. It shows that things connect and never shows a message, so nobody learns what actually crosses the wire.
mechanism: An AI app is sealed off from your tools and data. MCP standardizes the connection: a host runs one client per connection, and each client speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 to an MCP server over stdio or HTTP. A server exposes tools, resources, and prompts; after an initialize handshake the client lists what the server offers and the model can call a tool, whose result flows back into context.

anchor.what: host/client box on the left, server with its tools on the right, one JSON-RPC channel between them

worked_example.derivation: Bespoke integrations = M × N; with a shared protocol = M + N. Reduction factor = (M × N) / (M + N). Payloads are JSON.stringify'd from the objects above so they cannot drift.

beats.label: The wall
beats.caption: The app is boxed off from your tools and your data. It can talk, but it cannot act.
beats.idea: An AI app has no native access to external tools.
beats.focal_motion: host box and server box land; a wall rises between them

beats.label: M × N glue
beats.caption: Wire five apps to twenty tools by hand and you own a hundred connectors that never stop growing.
beats.focal_motion: a 5 × 20 grid of connector dots fills in, one row at a time

beats.label: One protocol
beats.caption: Put one shared protocol on the wire and the count collapses: twenty-five, not a hundred.
beats.idea: A shared protocol makes integration cost additive.
beats.focal_motion: the grid folds into a single row plus a single column

beats.label: Handshake
beats.caption: Initialize first. Client and server trade capabilities so each knows what the other can do.
beats.idea: A capability handshake opens the session.
beats.focal_motion: an initialize packet crosses the channel and a capabilities packet returns

beats.label: Discover
beats.caption: tools/list. The server advertises what it offers; here, one tool that takes a city name.
beats.idea: The client discovers the server's tools by listing them.
beats.focal_motion: the tools/list packet crosses; get_weather(city) appears on the server side

beats.label: Call a tool
beats.caption: The model asks for the weather. The client sends tools/call with the real arguments. The server runs it.
beats.idea: A tool call is a JSON-RPC request with named arguments.
beats.focal_motion: the tools/call payload crosses the channel; the server pulses as it executes

beats.label: Result returns
beats.caption: The result flows back as context. The model answers from live data, not from memory.
beats.idea: Results return over the same channel into the model's context.
beats.focal_motion: the result payload crosses back and lands in the host's context box

beats.label: Why it matters
beats.caption: Build the server once. Every host that speaks the protocol can call it. M plus N, not M times N.
beats.idea: Shared contracts stop integration from being combinatorial.
beats.focal_motion: the row-plus-column re-lights beside the two boxes; the wire glows

aha: Before MCP, every app wired itself to every tool by hand, M × N glue that never stopped growing. MCP makes the contract shared: a tool speaks the protocol once and every host can call it. Integration stops being combinatorial.

claims.text: An MCP server exposes tools, resources, and prompts.
A session begins with an initialize handshake, then list and call messages, all as JSON-RPC 2.0.
With a shared protocol the number of integrations is M + N rather than M × N.
